intro: Searching for an estate planning solicitor near you usually means you want to put your affairs in order, protect your family, or make sure your wishes are clearly set out. You might be thinking about a will, a trust, lasting powers of attorney, or how inheritance tax could affect what you leave behind. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who can discuss your situation and quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for an estate planning solicitor near me usually need
need_lead: Most people looking for an estate planning solicitor near me want clear, local advice on organising their affairs so their family and assets are protected.
needs: You want to write or update a will but are unsure how to account for your home, savings, and personal possessions.
You need to set up lasting powers of attorney so someone you trust can make decisions about your health and money if you cannot.
You are worried about inheritance tax and want to understand how trusts or other arrangements might help.
Your circumstances have changed after a marriage, divorce, bereavement, or new grandchild, and your existing plans need revisiting.
You want to make sure your original will is stored safely and that your executor knows where to find it.
context_heading: What to understand before you choose
context: Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors regulated by the SRA and chartered legal executives regulated by CILEx are insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman, and many estate planning specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly. When you speak to a professional, ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance, and where your original will will be stored.

If you live in Scotland, succession and confirmation follow different rules, so make sure any adviser you speak to practises in the right jurisdiction. Estate planning solicitors combine wills, trusts, lasting powers of attorney, and tax planning to protect your family and assets, and it is sensible to look at your plans again after major life events.

faqs.q: Do I need a solicitor to write a will?
faqs.a: You can write a will yourself, but a solicitor can help make sure it is clear and valid. Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity, so some will writers are not regulated, whereas solicitors are regulated and insured.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a will and lasting powers of attorney?
faqs.a: A will sets out what happens to your assets after you die, while lasting powers of attorney let you appoint someone to make decisions about your health and money during your lifetime if you lose capacity. Estate planning solicitors can advise on both together.

faqs.q: How can I check if an estate planning solicitor is regulated?
faqs.a: Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), and chartered legal executives by CILEx. You can ask the professional directly about their regulation and insurance, and check the relevant register.

faqs.q: Does it matter where the solicitor is based?
faqs.a: For most estate planning work, the law that applies depends on where you live, not where the solicitor is based. If you live in Scotland, make sure your adviser practises in Scottish succession rules, as they differ from England and Wales.

extra_heading: What happens at a first estate planning appointment
extra: A first meeting with an estate planning solicitor is mostly about gathering information rather than signing anything. You will usually be asked about your family, your home and other property, savings and investments, any business interests, and who you would want to benefit. It helps to bring a rough list of your assets and liabilities, plus any existing will or lasting powers of attorney, so the discussion starts from where you actually are.

The solicitor will then explain the options open to you, which may include a will, trusts, lasting powers of attorney for both health and money, and how inheritance tax could affect your estate. Expect to be asked about gifts you have already made and any property you own abroad, as these can change the picture. Nothing is decided at that first conversation unless you want it to be, and you are free to go away and think before committing.

Because quotes are given on application, ask at the outset how the professional charges and what the likely scope of work will be, so you can compare like with like. It is also worth asking who will actually handle your file and how they will keep in touch. If your circumstances are straightforward, the meeting may be short; if they are not, it may take longer and lead to a follow-up appointment.

extra_faqs.q: Should I bring anything to the first appointment?
extra_faqs.a: Bring a list of what you own and owe, details of your family, and any existing will or lasting powers of attorney. If you have made significant gifts or own property abroad, note those down too, as they affect the advice you will be given.

extra_faqs.q: Will the solicitor decide everything at the first meeting?
extra_faqs.a: No. The first appointment is usually for taking instructions and explaining your options, and you can take time to consider them. You should feel free to ask questions and to leave without committing until you are ready.

extra_faqs.q: How do I compare quotes for estate planning work?
extra_faqs.a: Ask each professional what their quote covers, whether it includes lasting powers of attorney as well as the will, and how they charge for any extra work. Comparing the scope alongside the price helps you judge which option suits you, rather than simply choosing the lowest figure.
